goal:
Clarify only the alternative-grammar section of the existing analysis below. Preserve its correct primary analysis and all eight observed form-meaning pairs. Make the proposed first-person agreement alternative fully explicit: choose the hypothetical marker, its position and person distribution; state any hypothetical pronoun needed; give one complete unattested sentence and the distinct predictions of the primary and alternative grammars. Clearly label invented forms as hypotheses, never new corpus evidence. Return only the replacement alternative-grammar section, directly as text. Do not repeat the full analysis, corpus glosses or requested translations. No tools, files, code or external research.

ORIGINAL CORPUS AND TASK (context, not additional work):
Act as a field linguist analyzing a deliberately fictional language, using only this complete corpus. Corpus: "kam velm tim" = "the lizard sees the owl"; "vel kamm dar" = "the owl follows the lizard"; "kami velm tim" = "the lizards see the owl"; "kam velim tim" = "the lizard sees the owls"; "sul kamm utim" = "the fox saw the lizard"; "veli sulm udar" = "the owls followed the fox"; "suli velim dar" = "the foxes follow the owls"; "vel sulim utim" = "the owl saw the foxes". Produce a careful linguistic analysis directly as text (no files, code, website or external research). Infer the smallest compositional lexicon and morphology accounting for all eight observations; show a morpheme-by-morpheme gloss for all eight; translate "the foxes saw the owls", "the lizard followed the foxes", "the owls see the lizards", and translate back "kami sulim udar". Distinguish observations from hypotheses. In particular explain whether these eight sentences establish negation, future tense, adjective order, or whether subject-verb agreement is absent for every person. Construct one explicit alternative grammar that agrees with all eight observed examples but differs on an unattested sentence, to demonstrate underdetermination. Do not invent additional corpus evidence.

EXISTING ANALYSIS:
Observations

The eight supplied examples consistently show subject–object–verb order. The recurring noun roots are kam ‘lizard’, vel ‘owl’, and sul ‘fox’. The recurring verb roots are tim ‘see’ and dar ‘follow’. Nouns with -i are translated as plural: kami ‘lizards’, veli ‘owls’, and suli ‘foxes’. Objects carry -m: velm, kamm, sulm, and sulim. The form -im is analyzable as plural -i plus object -m. Verbs beginning with u- are translated with past meanings: utim ‘saw’ and udar ‘followed’.

Proposed analysis

- kam = ‘lizard’; vel = ‘owl’; sul = ‘fox’
- tim = ‘see’; dar = ‘follow’
- -i = plural on nouns
- -m = object marking
- u- = past-tense marking on verbs
- constituent order = subject–object–verb

The English article ‘the’ occurs in the supplied translations, but the corpus does not establish a corresponding article morpheme.

Complete morpheme-by-morpheme glosses

1. kam velm tim
   kam vel-m tim
   lizard owl-OBJ see
   ‘the lizard sees the owl’

2. vel kamm dar
   vel kam-m dar
   owl lizard-OBJ follow
   ‘the owl follows the lizard’

3. kami velm tim
   kam-i vel-m tim
   lizard-PL owl-OBJ see
   ‘the lizards see the owl’

4. kam velim tim
   kam vel-i-m tim
   lizard owl-PL-OBJ see
   ‘the lizard sees the owls’

5. sul kamm utim
   sul kam-m u-tim
   fox lizard-OBJ PST-see
   ‘the fox saw the lizard’

6. veli sulm udar
   vel-i sul-m u-dar
   owl-PL fox-OBJ PST-follow
   ‘the owls followed the fox’

7. suli velim dar
   sul-i vel-i-m dar
   fox-PL owl-PL-OBJ follow
   ‘the foxes follow the owls’

8. vel sulim utim
   vel sul-i-m u-tim
   owl fox-PL-OBJ PST-see
   ‘the owl saw the foxes’

Requested translations

- ‘the foxes saw the owls’: suli velim utim
- ‘the lizard followed the foxes’: kam sulim udar
- ‘the owls see the lizards’: veli kamim tim
- kami sulim udar: ‘the lizards followed the foxes’

Evidential limits

These examples do not establish the form of negation, whether a future tense exists, adjective order, or that subject–verb agreement is absent for every person. They only show no overt verb variation across the noun-number combinations represented here.

Alternative grammar

An observationally equivalent grammar can retain the same roots, noun morphology, object marking, past prefix, and SOV order, while analyzing the observed verbs as carrying zero subject-person agreement for the third-person subjects represented in the corpus. It therefore matches all eight examples. For the unattested case ‘I see the owl’, this grammar predicts an overt first-person agreement marker on tim, whereas the simpler grammar predicts the invariant form tim. The corpus cannot distinguish these analyses.
